records.why: KICD outcome (e) asks for the area of a regular heptagon and octagon, and the KICD learning experiences ask learners to use regular-polygon objects from their surroundings. Only the octagon was taught. Check: 360 ÷ 7 = 51.43°, half-angle 25.71°, tan 25.71° = 0.4816, apothem = 2 ÷ 0.4816 = 4.15 m, area = 7 × ½ × 4 × 4.15 = 58.1 m²; the formula (7/4)s² cot(180°/7) = 1.75 × 16 × 2.0765 = 58.14 m² agrees.
records.old: PART E — Kericho Connection: Teacher asks: 'How does what we just did for the octagon help the Kericho community with their seven-sided plot?'
records.new: PART E — Kericho Connection: Teacher asks: 'How does what we just did for the octagon help the Kericho community with their seven-sided plot?' PART F — Regular heptagon and the world around us (fast finishers or homework): A regular heptagon has side 4 m. Learners use the same decomposition from the centre (seven congruent isosceles triangles, central angle 360° ÷ 7 ≈ 51.4°) with the apothem 4.15 m (given, or found as 2 ÷ tan 25.7° ≈ 2 ÷ 0.4816) to find its area: 7 × ½ × 4 × 4.15 ≈ 58.1 m². Learners also find one object or pattern at home or school shaped like a regular polygon (for example a hexagonal nut, an octagonal road sign or a hexagonal tile), measure its side, and estimate its area with the decomposition method.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry, Sub-Strand 2.5 Area of Polygons

records.value:
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner uses trigonometric ratios to generate the formula for a triangle given two sides and an included angle. In this sequence, the learner also decomposes complex irregular polygons into triangles and standard shapes to determine their areas, and applies these skills to real-life land and tiling problems in Kenyan contexts.
• Communication and Collaboration: the learner works in groups to measure, cut out and compare polygon shapes, discusses strategies for decomposing irregular polygons, and presents findings to peers.
• Creativity and Imagination: the learner identifies from the immediate environment objects in the shape of regular polygons and calculates their area. In this sequence, the learner also devises multiple methods (decomposition, formula, trigonometric) for finding the area of the same polygon and selects the most efficient approach.
• Learning to Learn: the learners research and discuss the use of the area of polygons in real-life situations. In this sequence, the learner also connects prior knowledge of triangles and quadrilaterals to build understanding of more complex polygons, and uses rulers, geometrical sets and calculators to verify results independently.
• Digital Literacy: the learner uses calculators and available digital devices to compute areas efficiently and to explore polygon area concepts through interactive tools.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry, Sub-Strand 2.5 Area of Polygons

records.why: KICD outcome (c) and the KICD content list 'area of a triangle using Heron's formula', but it appeared nowhere. Lesson 6 is where triangles from a drawing are measured, so it is the natural place; the 40-minute Lesson 3 is already full. The shoelace formula is not KICD content, so it is now optional. Checked: 6, 8, 10 gives s = 12 and 12 × 6 × 4 × 2 = 576, √576 = 24 = ½ × 6 × 8. Triangle ACD of the pentagon A(0,0), C(5,2), D(4,5) has sides √29 = 5.385, √10 = 3.162, √41 = 6.403, s = 7.475, area √(7.475 × 2.090 × 4.313 × 1.072) = 8.50 cm², which equals the shoelace/triangulation value ½|5×5 − 4×2| = 8.5. Teacher decides whether to run it as a whole-class segment (suggested) or to move it elsewhere.
records.old: Extension segment (~10 minutes, flagged as 'Challenge for Fast Finishers and Future Surveyors'): Teacher introduces the coordinate/shoelace formula.
records.new: HERON'S FORMULA segment (~8 minutes, whole class): The teacher asks: 'What if a surveyor can measure only the three sides of a triangle and has no way to get the height?' Learners use s = (a + b + c) ÷ 2 and A = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)]. First check on a 6 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm triangle: s = 12, A = √(12 × 6 × 4 × 2) = √576 = 24 cm², the same as ½ × 6 × 8. Then learners measure the three sides of triangle ACD on their shamba diagram (about 5.4 cm, 3.2 cm and 6.4 cm), apply Heron's formula (about 8.5 cm², small differences come from rounding the measured sides) and compare with their ½bh answer for ACD. Extension segment (optional, for Fast Finishers and Future Surveyors; not KICD content): Teacher introduces the coordinate/shoelace formula.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry, Sub-Strand 2.5 Area of Polygons

records.why: In triangle ABC, side b joins C and A, and side a joins B and C. A perpendicular from B to line CA makes a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse a and angle C, so sin C = h/a and A = ½bh = ½ab sin C. From vertex A the perpendicular lands on side a, which gives h = b sin C, not the sin C = h/a that Steps 2 to 4 and the teacher notes use. Checked with a = 5, b = 7, C = 58°: h from B = 5 × 0.8480 = 4.24, and ½ × 7 × 4.24 = 14.84 m².

records.why: In a rhombus both diagonals bisect each other, but in a kite only one diagonal is bisected, so 'same logic as rhombus' is wrong. What both shapes share is perpendicular diagonals. Kite ABCD with diagonal BD split by diagonal AC into parts p and q: triangles ABD and CBD have base BD = d₂ and heights p and q with p + q = AC = d₁, so area = ½d₂p + ½d₂q = ½d₁d₂. Check with a kite of diagonals 10 cm and 6 cm: 30 cm².
records.old: rhombus (each diagonal halves the other, giving four right-angle triangles), trapezium (two triangles with bases a and b sharing height h), and kite (same logic as rhombus).
records.new: rhombus (the diagonals cross at right angles and bisect each other, giving four congruent right-angled triangles with legs ½d₁ and ½d₂), trapezium (two triangles with bases a and b sharing height h), and kite (the diagonals cross at right angles; the diagonal d₂ splits the kite into two triangles with the same base d₂ whose heights add up to d₁, so A = ½d₂d₁).
records.reference: Euclidean geometry: area of a quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals (standard secondary mathematics textbooks, for example Kenya Literature Bureau Secondary Mathematics, area of quadrilaterals)

records.why: The apothem was stated without any reason, so the formula looked like a magic rule although the lesson says it is derived. Added the two-line reason using trigonometry from Sub-Strand 2.4. Checked: 1 ÷ (√2 − 1) = √2 + 1 = 2.4142 and 1.5 × 2.4142 = 3.62 m.
records.old: Each isosceles triangle has base s and height (apothem) = s/2 × (1 + √2).
records.new: Each isosceles triangle has base s and height (apothem) = s/2 × (1 + √2). (Split one triangle in half: the right-angled triangle has angle 22.5° and the side s/2 opposite it, so apothem = (s/2) ÷ tan 22.5°; since tan 22.5° = √2 − 1, 1 ÷ tan 22.5° = √2 + 1, and with s = 3 m this is 1.5 ÷ 0.4142 ≈ 3.62 m.)
records.reference: Standard geometry of regular polygons: apothem = s ÷ (2 tan(180°/n)), with tan 22.5° = √2 − 1

records.why: CBE rubrics have four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations) but the partner contract allows only three level fields, so Below Expectations cannot be represented in the Final Explanation rubric. Suggestion: teachers use 'Below Expectations' as the label for work that does not reach the Approaches descriptor, and the partner is asked whether a fourth field can be added.

KICD allocates 14 lessons to Sub-Strand 2.5 but this sequence has 8 lessons (600 minutes). Lessons cannot be added or removed, so every KICD outcome has been placed inside the 8 lessons (Heron's formula in Lesson 6, regular heptagon in Lesson 5), which makes Lessons 5 and 6 fuller. Teachers should confirm that this is acceptable, or plan extra practice lessons. The curriculum PDF used is the KICD Grade 10 Mathematics design; it is assumed to be the source for 'Core Mathematics'.
